study: Independent demand -> program-selected sources -> target HTTP comparison
issue_title: Author sort doesn't use any sort of normalization
issue_body: "China Miéville" sorts after "Kevin Mitnick" and "van der Whatever" sorts at the very end because lower case is sorted after upper case (or before or something, I don't know). We should be using natural sorts for these things that strip out diacritics and case normalize for sorting purposes (with tie-breakers going to the non-normalized version)
normative_sentence: We should be using natural sorts for these things that strip out diacritics and case normalize for sorting purposes (with tie-breakers going to the non-normalized version)
selection: Three literal need phrases generated by discover_sources.py; first 20 public GitHub repository results each; first three distinct sources in round-robin upstream order. No substitutions after source inspection.
human_contribution: Demand choice, acceptance interpretation, direct baseline and target integration adapters. Program chooses queries and candidate repositories. This is not autonomous contract construction or autonomous patch generation.
demand_choice: Chosen from the initial open-issue natural-sort search because it is a maintainer-authored unresolved bug with concrete examples and no named library. Other visible results included automated issue hunts, broad UI work, and a request explicitly naming a library; they were not selected. The engineer has general library knowledge, so no source-blind human claim is made.
mandatory: Author sort uses sort_name when present and name otherwise, as in the existing target.
Case differences and diacritics do not change the primary author ordering.
Equal normalized author names use original unnormalized text as tie-breaker.
Rendered author names remain unchanged, including accents and non-Latin text.
Ascending/descending order, pagination and repeated cached HTTP requests are consistent.
Existing title/date ordering and fallback fields are preserved outside the author-key correction.
interpretation: Canonical Unicode NFD decomposition, remove combining marks, then casefold is the direct interpretation. The issue does not specify locale collation, transliteration or numeric author labels; these are not silently added as mandatory demands. For multiple authors retain the existing ordered-list comparison, replacing each string with (normalized, original).
direct_baseline: A small target-local key implemented with Python unicodedata.normalize, unicodedata.combining and str.casefold, with the original string as the secondary key. Compare against this full solution, not only the broken target or a weak lowercase-only shortcut.
measurement: Original target, direct correction and at most three selected-source adapters use the same real application routes, database records, templates and HTTP assertions. No mocked sorter, renderer or response. Record failures. Measure nine fresh-sort HTTP latencies on 1000 and 10000 authors with only the target's book cache cleared between runs, identical data and alternating variant order. Report medians and dependency costs; no test-set tuning.
benefit_gate: All mandatory HTTP cases and target regressions must pass. Benefit requires either mandatory correctness that the best direct implementation cannot provide, or at least 20 percent lower median fresh-sort HTTP latency at both sizes without more than 10 percent regression in warm HTTP latency. Fewer adapter lines alone, popularity, an isolated sandbox pass and matching text do not establish benefit. Adoption and user acceptance remain unknown.
stop: Do not replace rejected repositories, expand API grammar, tune search phrases after retrieval, introduce new infrastructure, or spend AI API budget. An all-negative result is permitted. Historical evidence remains unchanged. No publication to the target project's maintainers.
